title: How I Stumbled Into Code
content:
“Yesterday is history, tomorrow is a mystery,
but today is a gift - that’s why it’s called the present.”

  • Master Oogway

Back Then

The Block Era

The first time I encountered “programming” was when I was about 10 years old. I was never the type of kid who studied hard - I was always looking for fun. One day, after watching some Minecraft gameplay videos online, I overheard my classmates talking about their computer programming class.

Programming? That sounded like I could become a developer and create my own mods to play with in games, I thought. Little did I know, this was where my fate with the world of code began.

Amusing myself was the first thing I did. With blocks combined and divided, I could build mini games the same as those browser-based H5 games, make short animations back then, even create poll tools that only had a front-end site - something I didn’t realise was a real class until years later, and so on. That class built my coding logic through these playful, childlike exercises. To be frank, I can’t imagine how hard the subsequent learning would have been without this logic. I always find it hard to get through to people when teaching programming - what came naturally to me through block programming, they just couldn’t grasp. They need to see my written code to follow this concise, start-to-end thinking. I need a long time and more effort to build programming logic in them. Yet even that felt shallow - I wanted to write it myself, not explain it. However, I felt it was not enough. Meanwhile, the coding shouldn’t be like moving blocks and clicking the start button - pioneers didn’t have any kits like this. I wanted to stand by their side. As Isaac Newton once put it: “If I have seen further, it is by standing on the shoulders of giants.”

Real Code, Real Languages

After a year, I asked my parent to bring me to another programming class. There, my coding life really began - with JavaScript.

Flight fighter. That was the name of the game - one of the most popular 2D air war games back then. Users can play it on their phone without downloading anything. And in the first class of my new programming center, the teacher opened it up and typed something like “life = -1” on the board. The plane stopped dying. That single line of code rewrote the rules of the game. I sat there, stunned. So this was what code could do. I wanted to do it myself.

So I started writing JavaScript. I still remember typing ‘ctx.fillText()’ for the first time and watching the browser actually print my words on the screen. It felt like directing - I was the director, the canvas was my stage, and every line of the code was an actor. That was my first real taste of front-end thinking: stage, canvas,layer. There were hidden games too. I found games that previous students had stashed in the public computer. During breaks, I’d play them and wonder - how did they hide these files? Curiosity led me to encryption and file systems, years before I knew those terms. The JS chapter closed with a competition. Three hours, one project. I didn’t finish everything. 3rd prize. But that wasn’t the point. The point was: this phase was fun. Light, exciting, full of small victories. Now, years later, I can still read JS - but writing it feels distant, like a language I once spoke fluently. The front-end mindset it planted stayed, though. The idea of a stage. The joy of making things appear on screen. That was the real beginning.

The Cliff Edge

I was full of passion at first. Until then, despite only winning 3rd prize, I hadn’t yet run into any problems I couldn’t solve even after seeing the answers. I suddenly joined the C++ road, carrying my pounding heart.

My C++ journey started with muscle memory. I needed to memorize head files, namespaces,the main function and return 0;. I never timed myself, but I know I can write all of that in 10 seconds even now. To be frank, C++'s basic structure had become a marco to me - a marco I think I’ll carry to my tomb.

As humans climb hills, C++ is also like a mountain of computer world. It is easy at first, printing an asterisk triangle, calculate using some rules, dividing numbers and reversing them. It sounds like a strategy game. Just as I had done many times in the Block era. Through loops and branch structures, I could easily figure out the problems. All I needed to do was do what the problem said, or I worked out the problem and write my mind down in C++ phrases. But the problems wouldn’t always be so simple. It would take a bit more time to understand sort algorithm like bubble sort - the easiest sort algorithm nearly every programmer first met in algorithm field. I regarded it as a crab - which took me some time but wasn’t a mountain. Then I met more and more crabs. Divided sort, fast sort, shell sort, inject sort, stack structure, queue structure and tree. If other crabs are mitten-handed crabs - small, manageable, pinch-y but doable - then trees must be the emperor crabs: the mountain itself, the peak I had to climb. I knew sometimes it was yummy and elegant. But when DFS and BFS came along. I felt a horror, a horror for no matter how many times I read the code I couldn’t understand its logic. I couldn’t understand its jump thinking.

I have to admit that tree algorithm really beat me. I lost the game - temporarily.

I lost, I couldn’t understand it, and I hadn’t won a prize in the competition this time. I thought I had totally failed. It seemed like kids should just act like kids, not spend every day on computers. And parents could easily lock away all electronic devices. I went back to a boring study life, not thinking about that exciting experience anymore. I was even unwilling to hear messages from that field. But as a movie said: “I have to remind myself that some birds aren’t meant to be caged. Their feathers are just too bright. And when they fly away, the part of you that knows it was a sin to lock them up DOES rejoice. Still, the place you live in is that much more drab and empty that they’re gone.” – Stephen King Three years later, I quietly stepped away from computers. I came back. Maybe I still remembered the first reason I joined. Maybe I still admired using computers to do the things others couldn’t. Maybe I just wanted to take a nap that time. Maybe I found that a machine was more trustworthy than real people. Also, the teacher said python could be a part of our exam. Due to many reasons, I came back.

This time, things had changed. No need to care about parents. Not just a personal hobby. Python had joined to official examination, which was a part of exam score if anyone chose. Tech lover had gathered. I finally found my advantages. I had a programming logic better than most of students because I had loved it many years since Block Era. How could I give up? Plus, I loved machine. That was enough! I didn’t have too much friends, and was lonely for many days. A trusted, fully controlled machine was the best to deal with times. Never betrayed! I was 16 that time, the year Novel AI was born. I saw beautiful pictures every day. Then ChatGPT came out. Both the world and I were crazy about that. When I sat there, I was not lonely anymore. If I could do more, I could code more. I couldn’t bear not understanding intelligent machines. So for better grades and a dream of meeting a machine angel. I came back again.

Even though I changed language this time. It was easy for me to learn programming. I found everything went easier for me when I grew up. 3 years break time inspired my ideas. I found programming languages were not important. There was a philosophy in this action. I only needed to be aware of efficiency and the methods. I mastered Python basics in nearly an afternoon. I finally found my lost confidence.

Right Now

Look now, I have my blog. The cliff edge is gone. Indeed, a restart programming life wasn’t so easy. Sounds like an idiot. I had read C and C++ textbook 3 times in 2 different languages and 3 editions. The last time felt like a swordfish slightly moving in the ocean. To this day, I am caring about new frontiers - not only reviewing C and C++, but also exploring Azure, flutter, golang, Linux system, AWS, game server and more. All in all, when I picked up those knowledge and downloaded an IDE again, I could feel a power that not lead by teachers, not pushed by parents, only within my heart. I didn’t need to be sad for my time away and memory loss, because this restart would recreate them all. I will do better. When I was still learning JavaScript, I heard that the real master could build their project through notebook. By the time I downloaded vim and called clang , javac, rustc…from shell command. I had already become a master. I didn’t know when I finished such restart. I guess it took me maybe 2 years. I was just too busy in high school. I might not have been a winner at school. My grade hadn’t brought me to an university that I am honored by. But I am keeping my pace. I wouldn’t stop my steps again.

What’s Next

Technology is boosting. As all storytime ended, listeners offered their comments or just fell asleep. I don’t know what future would be. I won’t stop my steps. Maybe one day I can’t coding again. But I know, ended is another beginning, death is another birth. This blog is coming to an end. While our story is still going. Maybe my dream like future will come. Maybe horrible sci-fi ending will come. I don’t know and I don’t care. I just want a better life.

For all newcomers: Rome is not built in a day. You would absolutely meet difficulty, tough challenges, and obstacles when you were trying to do serious things - to make a useful tools. There might be no one who could help you, no one could understand you, no one could stand behind you. You can suspend it temporarily. You can keep fighting with it. You can do whatever you want. Well, don’t be silly. Never forget why you did this. Never regret about doing an awesome things. And today is still a gift.
